claim: Twenty-seven patients (14 male, 18–50 years, 8 left handed) participated in the experiments.
source: Twenty-seven patients (14 male, 18–50 years, 8 left handed) participated in the experiments after written informed consent was obtained.
evidence: Direct statement of participant demographics from the study cohort.

claim: The posterior insula was robustly active bilaterally, but after the onset of articulation.
source: The posterior insula was robustly active bilaterally, but after the onset of articulation, during listening to speech and during production of non-speech mouth movements.
evidence: Experimental observation from intracranial electrode recordings during speech tasks.

claim: The posterior insula was active during listening to speech.
source: The posterior insula was robustly active bilaterally, but after the onset of articulation, during listening to speech and during production of non-speech mouth movements.
evidence: Experimental observation from intracranial electrode recordings during listening task.

claim: The posterior insula was active during production of non-speech mouth movements.
source: The posterior insula was robustly active bilaterally, but after the onset of articulation, during listening to speech and during production of non-speech mouth movements.
evidence: Experimental observation from intracranial electrode recordings during orofacial praxis task.

claim: Preceding articulation there was very sparse activity in the insula, localized primarily to the frontal operculum rather than the insula.
source: Preceding articulation there was very sparse activity, localized primarily to the frontal operculum rather than the insula.
evidence: Experimental observation from temporal analysis of electrode recordings before speech onset.

claim: Posterior insula was active coincident with superior temporal gyrus.
source: Posterior insular was active coincident with superior temporal gyrus but was more active for self-generated speech than external speech, the opposite of the superior temporal gyrus.
evidence: Temporal comparison of activation patterns between posterior insula and STG during speech tasks.

claim: Posterior insula was more active for self-generated speech than external speech.
source: Posterior insular was active coincident with superior temporal gyrus but was more active for self-generated speech than external speech, the opposite of the superior temporal gyrus.
evidence: Comparison of activation amplitudes between reading and listening tasks in posterior insula.

claim: Superior temporal gyrus was more active for external speech than self-generated speech.
source: Posterior insular was active coincident with superior temporal gyrus but was more active for self-generated speech than external speech, the opposite of the superior temporal gyrus.
evidence: Comparison of activation amplitudes between reading and listening tasks in STG.

claim: The insula does not serve pre-articulatory preparatory roles.
source: These findings support the conclusion that the insula does not serve pre-articulatory preparatory roles.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from temporal analysis showing lack of pre-articulatory activity in insula.

claim: Multiple lesion studies have linked insular damage to apraxia of speech (AOS).
source: Multiple lesion studies have linked insular damage to speech and orofacial motor control disorders such as apraxia of speech (AOS) (Dronkers, 1996; Marien et al., 2001; Ogar et al., 2006; Itabashi et al., 2016), dysarthria (Baier et al., 2011) and dysphagia (Daniels et al., 1996).
evidence: Referenced prior lesion studies linking insular damage to AOS.

claim: Multiple lesion studies have linked insular damage to dysarthria.
source: Multiple lesion studies have linked insular damage to speech and orofacial motor control disorders such as apraxia of speech (AOS) (Dronkers, 1996; Marien et al., 2001; Ogar et al., 2006; Itabashi et al., 2016), dysarthria (Baier et al., 2011) and dysphagia (Daniels et al., 1996).
evidence: Referenced prior lesion studies linking insular damage to dysarthria.

claim: Multiple lesion studies have linked insular damage to dysphagia.
source: Multiple lesion studies have linked insular damage to speech and orofacial motor control disorders such as apraxia of speech (AOS) (Dronkers, 1996; Marien et al., 2001; Ogar et al., 2006; Itabashi et al., 2016), dysarthria (Baier et al., 2011) and dysphagia (Daniels et al., 1996).
evidence: Referenced prior lesion studies linking insular damage to dysphagia.

claim: Dronkers' study found a 100% lesion overlap in the left superior precentral gyrus of the insula in AOS patients.
source: Dronkers' study was the first to quantitatively link anterior insular damage to a disruption in speech production, finding a 100% lesion overlap in the left superior precentral gyrus of the insula (SPG) in AOS patients.
evidence: Summary of findings from Dronkers' lesion study.

claim: Lesion symptom mapping revealed that patients with SPG lesions produced a greater number of speech errors during complex, multisyllabic articulations.
source: Lesion symptom mapping revealed that patients with SPG lesions produced a greater number of speech errors during complex, multisyllabic articulations (Ogar et al., 2006; Baldo et al., 2011).
evidence: Referenced findings from lesion symptom mapping studies.

claim: fMRI studies implicate the anterior insula in both speech perception and production.
source: Further evidence was contributed by fMRI studies that implicate the anterior insula in both speech perception and production (Mutschler et al., 2009; Adank, 2012; McGettigan et al., 2013; Ardila et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: Referenced fMRI studies showing anterior insula activation during speech tasks.

claim: In the dual-stream model of the speech articulation network, the anterior insula is included as part of the putative dorsal sensorimotor pathway.
source: In the dual-stream model of the speech articulation network, the anterior insula is included as part of the putative dorsal sensorimotor pathway (Hickok and Poeppel, 2007).
evidence: Referenced theoretical model of speech articulation network.

claim: Comparative assessments of activation to speech and non-speech oral movements have shown greater activity for non-speech within the insula.
source: Comparative assessments of activation to speech and non-speech oral movements have shown greater activity for non-speech within the insula (Bonilha et al., 2006) suggesting a more general role in oral motor control without specialization for speech.
evidence: Referenced comparative study of speech vs. non-speech oral movements.

claim: The apparent involvement of the SPG in complex articulation might actually be attributable to the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG).
source: Also, it has been suggested that the apparent involvement of the SPG in complex articulation might actually be attributable to the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (Fedorenko et al., 2015), therefore the insula's engagement based on AOS lesion studies may simply reflect the high probability of insular damage following middle cerebral artery ischemia, with Broca's area lesions being more causative of AOS (Hillis et al., 2004).
evidence: Referenced alternative interpretation of lesion data.

claim: Somatosensory manifestations occur in 70% of cases during insular stimulation.
source: Of the many patients who have undergone insular stimulation with implanted electrodes, somatosensory manifestations are relatively common (in 70% of cases), but speech disruptions occur very infrequently (5–7% of the time) (Ostrowsky et al., 2000; Afif et al., 2010; Pugnaghi et al., 2011; Stephani et al., 2011; Mazzola et al., 2017).
evidence: Referenced stimulation studies reporting frequency of somatosensory manifestations.

claim: Speech disruptions occur in 5–7% of cases during insular stimulation.
source: Of the many patients who have undergone insular stimulation with implanted electrodes, somatosensory manifestations are relatively common (in 70% of cases), but speech disruptions occur very infrequently (5–7% of the time) (Ostrowsky et al., 2000; Afif et al., 2010; Pugnaghi et al., 2011; Stephani et al., 2011; Mazzola et al., 2017).
evidence: Referenced stimulation studies reporting frequency of speech disruptions.

claim: Task accuracy for the word reading task was 96.4 ± 5.3%.
source: Task accuracy for the word reading task was 96.4 ± 5.3% (mean ± SD) with an average response time (RT) of 978 ± 221 ms from word presentation.
evidence: Behavioral performance data from the word reading task.

claim: The average response time for the word reading task was 978 ± 221 ms from word presentation.
source: Task accuracy for the word reading task was 96.4 ± 5.3% (mean ± SD) with an average response time (RT) of 978 ± 221 ms from word presentation.
evidence: Behavioral performance data from the word reading task.

claim: The response time for the object naming task was 1192 ± 245 ms.
source: The RT for the object naming task was 1192 ± 245 ms.
evidence: Behavioral performance data from the object naming task.

claim: 75.1 ± 10.6% of responses in the naming task had both correct articulation and the expected, most common word choice.
source: 75.1 ± 10.6% of responses in the naming task had both correct articulation and the expected, most common word choice; only these were used for subsequent analysis.
evidence: Behavioral performance data from the naming task.

claim: IFG activation began ~750 ms before speech onset, prior to CS activation.
source: IFG activation began ~750 ms before speech onset, prior to CS activation.
evidence: Temporal analysis of electrode recordings showing IFG activation timing.

claim: CS activity was maximal at speech onset.
source: CS activity was maximal at speech onset and, shortly after the onset speech, STG became active.
evidence: Temporal analysis of electrode recordings showing CS activation timing.

claim: Shortly after the onset of speech, STG became active.
source: CS activity was maximal at speech onset and, shortly after the onset speech, STG became active.
evidence: Temporal analysis of electrode recordings showing STG activation timing.

claim: There were no differences in the amplitude of activation in posterior insula between simple monosyllabic names vs. complex read words.
source: There were no differences in the amplitude of activation with varying levels of articulation complexity - simple monosyllabic names vs. complex read words (Wilcoxon rank sign, 200–600 ms; p=0.083) and multisyllabic naming responses (p=0.898) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical comparison of activation amplitudes across different articulation complexities.

claim: There were no differences in the amplitude of activation in posterior insula between simple monosyllabic names and multisyllabic naming responses.
source: There were no differences in the amplitude of activation with varying levels of articulation complexity - simple monosyllabic names vs. complex read words (Wilcoxon rank sign, 200–600 ms; p=0.083) and multisyllabic naming responses (p=0.898) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical comparison of activation amplitudes across different articulation complexities.

claim: Longer articulation times resulted in longer activation duration for multisyllabic words in posterior insula.
source: The only difference observed was a duration effect, with longer articulation times and therefore longer activation duration for multisyllabic words (600–1000 ms; p=0.024).
evidence: Statistical analysis of activation duration across different word lengths.

claim: The STG responded more strongly to external speech than to self-generated speech.
source: As expected, from other studies of auditory cortex, the STG responded more strongly to external speech than to self-generated speech (p=0.002) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical comparison of STG activation between listening and reading tasks.

claim: The posterior insula showed a significantly greater response during speech production than during speech listening.
source: The posterior insula, however, showed a significantly greater response during speech production than during speech listening (p=0.019), thus these two adjacent regions are functional dissociable.
evidence: Statistical comparison of posterior insula activation between reading and listening tasks.

claim: In the praxis task, significant post-articulatory activation was observed in posterior insula where none was seen in STG.
source: Further, in the praxis task, we observed significant post-articulatory activation in posterior insula where none was seen in STG (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparison of activation patterns between posterior insula and STG during orofacial praxis task.

claim: The anterior insula showed a very weak though significant activation in both speech articulation tasks, starting shortly after the IFG.
source: The anterior insula showed a very weak though significant activation in both speech articulation tasks, starting shortly after the IFG.
evidence: Temporal and amplitude analysis of anterior insula activation during speech tasks.

claim: Anterior insula activation first became significant around 150 ms before speech onset and remained active for the duration of speech.
source: This low amplitude response first became significant around 150 ms before speech onset and remained active for the duration of speech, concurrent with the posterior insula and STG.
evidence: Temporal analysis of anterior insula activation during speech tasks.

claim: No significant evoked activity was observed in anterior insula.
source: Additionally, when considering the evoked activity from anterior insula, we observed no significant response (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Event-related potential analysis of anterior insula during speech tasks.

claim: In the post-articulatory period of both the reading and naming tasks, the posterior insula, bilaterally along the anterior long gyri (ALG), showed clusters of electrodes responding with high significance and amplitude, primarily in the superior part of the gyrus.
source: In the post-articulatory period of both the reading and naming tasks, the posterior insula, bilaterally along the anterior long gyri (ALG), showed clusters of electrodes responding with high significance and amplitude, primarily in the superior part of the gyrus (Figure 3B; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Individual electrode analysis showing spatial distribution of activation in posterior insula.

claim: The posterior insula region was the primary region of activation in the listening task.
source: This region also appeared to be the primary region of activation in the listening task and also showed significant but low amplitude activation during the praxis task.
evidence: Individual electrode analysis showing activation patterns across different tasks.

claim: The posterior insula showed significant but low amplitude activation during the praxis task.
source: This region also appeared to be the primary region of activation in the listening task and also showed significant but low amplitude activation during the praxis task.
evidence: Individual electrode analysis showing activation patterns during orofacial praxis task.

claim: In the pre-articulatory period, prominent activity was seen in the IFG and a cluster across the medial frontal operculum but little to no significant activity anywhere in the insula.
source: In the pre-articulatory period, we saw prominent activity in the IFG and a cluster across the medial frontal operculum but little to no significant activity anywhere in the insula.
evidence: Surface-based mixed-effects multilevel analysis (sb-MEMA) showing spatial distribution of pre-articulatory activity.

claim: In the post-articulatory time period, the majority of posterior insula showed substantial activation, accompanied by a large activation across the STG.
source: By comparison, in the post-articulatory time period, the majority of posterior insula showed substantial activation, accompanied by a large activation across the STG.
evidence: Surface-based mixed-effects multilevel analysis (sb-MEMA) showing spatial distribution of post-articulatory activity.

claim: The activation cluster in the post-articulatory period extended across the frontal operculum and spread into part of the superior anterior insula.
source: Additionally, the activation cluster extended across the frontal operculum and spread into part of the superior anterior insula.
evidence: Surface-based mixed-effects multilevel analysis (sb-MEMA) showing spatial extent of post-articulatory activation.

claim: FO electrodes showed significant gamma activation that started up to 700 ms before articulation and continued for the duration of articulation.
source: FO electrodes showed significant gamma activation that started up to 700 ms before articulation and continued for the duration of articulation (Figure 5A,B; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Analysis of frontal operculum electrode recordings during speech tasks.

claim: The band-limited (70–150 Hz) voltage traces of AI and FO electrode pairs were significantly correlated.
source: The band-limited (70–150 Hz) voltage traces of these electrodes were significantly correlated between the electrode pairs (r = 0.11 ± 0.03, mean ± SE; Wilcoxon rank sign, p=0.008), this correlation was maximal at 0 ms time lag, suggestive of volume conduction between the two regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cross-correlation analysis of voltage traces between AI and FO electrodes.

claim: The correlation between AI and FO electrode pairs was maximal at 0 ms time lag, suggestive of volume conduction between the two regions.
source: The band-limited (70–150 Hz) voltage traces of these electrodes were significantly correlated between the electrode pairs (r = 0.11 ± 0.03, mean ± SE; Wilcoxon rank sign, p=0.008), this correlation was maximal at 0 ms time lag, suggestive of volume conduction between the two regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cross-correlation analysis showing zero time lag between AI and FO signals.

claim: Significantly larger responses were seen along the entire left STG to externally generated over self-generated speech.
source: However, when we compared the response amplitudes between the reading and listening tasks, within individual electrodes (Figure 6; Figure 6—source data 1), significantly larger responses were seen along the entire left STG to externally generated over self-generated speech.
evidence: Within-electrode comparison of activation amplitudes between reading and listening tasks in STG.

claim: The posterior insula showed greater activation during self-generated speech compared to externally generated speech.
source: By contrast, the posterior insula showed greater activation during self-generated speech.
evidence: Within-electrode comparison of activation amplitudes between reading and listening tasks in posterior insula.

claim: Band-limited voltage traces in PI-STG electrode pairs were not significantly correlated.
source: In contrast to the AI-FO correlation, band-limited voltage traces in these electrode pairs were not significantly correlated (r = 0.01 ± 0.03, mean ± SE; Wilcoxon rank sign, p=0.74).
evidence: Cross-correlation analysis of voltage traces between PI and STG electrodes.

claim: Bilateral posterior insula, particularly the superior anterior long gyri, appear involved in some aspect of monitoring during speech production.
source: Rather, bilateral posterior insula, particularly the superior anterior long gyri, appear involved in some aspect of monitoring during speech production, a process that is functionally separable from that of the superior temporal gyrus.
evidence: Synthesis of experimental findings regarding posterior insula function.

claim: There is little evidence anterior insula is directly involved in speech or language production.
source: We find little evidence anterior insula is directly involved in speech or language production, with the neighboring frontal operculum more likely being the true regional activity source.
evidence: Synthesis of experimental findings regarding anterior insula function.

claim: The neighboring frontal operculum is more likely being the true regional activity source for speech production.
source: We find little evidence anterior insula is directly involved in speech or language production, with the neighboring frontal operculum more likely being the true regional activity source.
evidence: Synthesis of experimental findings regarding frontal operculum function.

claim: The weaker activation in posterior insula during constituent components of speech compared with speech production could suggest that this region may serve a role in integration of auditory and somatosensory input.
source: The weaker activation during these constituent components of speech compared with speech production could suggest that this region may serve a role in integration of auditory and somatosensory input (Rodgers et al., 2008).
evidence: Interpretation of activation patterns with reference to prior literature on sensory integration.

claim: The activation profile in posterior insula could suggest its involvement in respiratory or laryngeal control.
source: It could also suggest its involvement in respiratory or laryngeal control (Ackermann and Riecker, 2010; Fedorenko et al., 2015), aspects we did not control for in these experiments.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of activation patterns with reference to prior literature.

claim: Auditory cortex is suppressed during self-generated speech.
source: It is well known that auditory cortex is suppressed during self-generated speech (Creutzfeldt et al., 1989; Paus et al., 1996; Numminen et al., 1999; Chan et al., 2014) and self-generated sounds more generally (Rummell et al., 2016; Singla et al., 2017), likely as a result of interactions between auditory and non-auditory sensory feedback in auditory cortex.
evidence: Referenced prior studies showing auditory cortex suppression during self-generated speech.

claim: Posterior insular activity does not suppress in response to articulation.
source: While STG is more active during externally produced speech than self-generated speech, posterior insular activity does not suppress in response to articulation and rather, is more active during self-generated speech.
evidence: Comparison of activation patterns between STG and posterior insula during speech tasks.

claim: The notion that the posterior insula is involved in somatosensory processing is broadly consistent with lesional studies of dysarthric and dysphagic populations.
source: The notion of that the posterior insula is involved in somatosensory processing is broadly consistent with lesional studies of dysarthric (Baier et al., 2011) and dysphagic (Daniels et al., 1996) populations and with stimulation studies that result in orofacial sensations (Pugnaghi et al., 2011).
evidence: Interpretation of findings in context of prior lesion and stimulation studies.

claim: The notion that the posterior insula is involved in somatosensory processing is broadly consistent with stimulation studies that result in orofacial sensations.
source: The notion of that the posterior insula is involved in somatosensory processing is broadly consistent with lesional studies of dysarthric (Baier et al., 2011) and dysphagic (Daniels et al., 1996) populations and with stimulation studies that result in orofacial sensations (Pugnaghi et al., 2011).
evidence: Interpretation of findings in context of prior stimulation studies.

claim: Given the lack of pre-articulatory activity shown in this study and the lack of any relationship of activation to the complexity of articulation, it is unlikely that lesions of the posterior insula are crucial for AOS.
source: Given the lack of pre-articulatory activity shown in this study and the lack of any relationship of activation to the complexity of articulation, it is unlikely that lesions of this region are crucial for AOS.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental findings regarding AOS etiology.

claim: The findings best support AOS representing a disruption of the IFG.
source: Thus, our findings best support AOS representing a disruption of the IFG (Hillis et al., 2004; Fedorenko et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental findings with reference to prior literature on AOS.

claim: The findings are suggestive of posterior insula as a sensory monitoring region.
source: Taken together these findings are suggestive of a sensory monitoring region - congruent with the role of the insula in auditory-somatosensory integration (Rodgers et al., 2008) where both auditory and somatosensory activity in rodent insula is maximal during coincident presentation, comparable to what we see during human self-generated speech.
evidence: Synthesis of experimental findings with reference to prior literature on sensory integration.

claim: The frontal operculum is the only peri-insular region in this study with significant and substantial pre-articulatory gamma activity.
source: The frontal operculum is also the only peri-insular region in this study with significant and substantial pre-articulatory gamma activity, the timing of which would implicate it as a preparatory region, a role that has traditionally been attributed to the insula.
evidence: Analysis of frontal operculum activation timing during speech tasks.

claim: The timing of frontal operculum activity would implicate it as a preparatory region.
source: The frontal operculum is also the only peri-insular region in this study with significant and substantial pre-articulatory gamma activity, the timing of which would implicate it as a preparatory region, a role that has traditionally been attributed to the insula.
evidence: Inference drawn from temporal analysis of frontal operculum activation.

claim: Disruption of the frontal operculum has been shown to lead to language disruption.
source: This agrees with stimulation studies of the operculum as disruption of this region has been shown to lead to language disruption (Mălîia et al., 2018).
evidence: Referenced stimulation study showing language disruption from operculum stimulation.

claim: Electrodes have a center-to-center separation of ~4 mm.
source: Our electrodes have a center-to-center separation of ~4 mm and this distance between neighboring electrodes allowed us to distinguish the highly active frontal operculum from the minimally active anterior insula.
evidence: Description of electrode spacing used in the study.

claim: In most modern fMRI, a smoothing kernel of 4–8 mm is used.
source: In most modern fMRI, a smoothing kernel of 4–8 mm is used (Mikl et al., 2008) which would likely remove the distinction between these two regions.
evidence: Referenced typical fMRI smoothing parameters.

claim: fMRI smoothing of 4-8 mm would likely remove the distinction between frontal operculum and anterior insula.
source: In most modern fMRI, a smoothing kernel of 4–8 mm is used (Mikl et al., 2008) which would likely remove the distinction between these two regions.
evidence: Inference about the effect of fMRI smoothing on spatial resolution.

claim: All experimental procedures were reviewed and approved by the Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects (CPHS) of the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston as Protocol Number HSC-MS-06–0385.
source: All experimental procedures were reviewed and approved by the Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects (CPHS) of the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston as Protocol Number HSC-MS-06–0385.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval for the study.

claim: Inclusion criteria were that the participants were an English native speaker, had at least one electrode contact localized in the insular long or short gyri and that the insula was not identified as a seizure onset zone.
source: Inclusion criteria were that the participants were an English native speaker, had at least one electrode contact localized in the insular long or short gyri and that the insula was not identified as a seizure onset zone.
evidence: Description of participant inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: 52 electrodes in 20 patients were localized to anterior insula.
source: 52 electrodes in 20 patients were localized to anterior insula (LH n = 40 (16), RH n = 12 (5); # electrodes (# patients)) and 53 electrodes in 14 patients were localized to posterior insula (LH n = 30 (9), RH n = 23 (7)).
evidence: Description of electrode localization to anterior insula.

claim: 53 electrodes in 14 patients were localized to posterior insula.
source: 52 electrodes in 20 patients were localized to anterior insula (LH n = 40 (16), RH n = 12 (5); # electrodes (# patients)) and 53 electrodes in 14 patients were localized to posterior insula (LH n = 30 (9), RH n = 23 (7)).
evidence: Description of electrode localization to posterior insula.

claim: All words used in the reading task had three or more syllables, an initial CCV phoneme structure, and a high articulatory travel.
source: To create high articulatory complexity and to maximally engage the insula (Baldo et al., 2011), all words used had three or more syllables, an initial CCV phoneme structure, and a high articulatory travel (e.g. snapdragon, globalization, claustrophobia).
evidence: Description of stimulus design for the reading task.

claim: In the reading task, articulation onset preceded audible speech by 108 ± 127 ms.
source: This comparison showed that in the reading task, articulation onset preceded audible speech by 108 ± 127 ms.
evidence: Video analysis comparing articulation onset to audible speech onset.

claim: A total of 5312 electrode contacts were implanted in these patients.
source: A total of 5312 electrode contacts were implanted in these patients, 1807 of these were excluded from analysis due to proximity to the seizure onset zone, excessive inter-ictal spikes or line noise.
evidence: Description of total electrode coverage across all patients.

claim: 1807 electrode contacts were excluded from analysis due to proximity to the seizure onset zone, excessive inter-ictal spikes or line noise.
source: A total of 5312 electrode contacts were implanted in these patients, 1807 of these were excluded from analysis due to proximity to the seizure onset zone, excessive inter-ictal spikes or line noise.
evidence: Description of electrode exclusion criteria and numbers.
